title: Pricing framing and discount guidance
body:
Purpose:
This is a working draft to align messaging and guardrails for Redwood’s public pricing page, sales one-pagers, and renewal conversations. Focus areas: metric framing (what customers compare), an evidence-backed case for token-based metering, recommended tier constructs, and practical discounting language and rules.

Framing hypothesis (short):
Buyers care about three things when choosing an inference vendor: predictable unit economics, control over tail costs, and measurable quality. Our messaging should put unit economics first, then show how tokens map to application outcomes and how Redwood’s controls (batching, caching, routing) reduce effective unit cost.

Which metrics to lead with (customer-facing):
- Effective cost per 1k user-visible characters or per 1k tokens (primary): easy to calculate from sample prompts.
- Latency SLOs by route/model: p50/p95 in ms for common request shapes.
- Cost per concurrent request (for scale buyers) or cost per 1M tokens (for price-sensitive buyers).
- Quality uplift band (optional callout): model family + sample eval delta vs common baseline.

Why token metering (how to explain simply to customers):
- Precision: Tokens give a fine-grained signal tied to compute and therefore cost. Charging by API call or result size masks compute differences (long context vs short).
- Predictability: With clear per-token units customers can map prompts to spend and reason about changes (e.g., longer context = X% more cost).
- Alignment: Tokens align with the optimizations we offer (prefix caching, KV reuse, quantized models) — tracking tokens makes those savings visible to customers.
- Practical shorthand for customers: Provide a short conversion chart (approx chars -> tokens, typical patterns) so they can estimate without model internals.

Plain-language customer copy examples (use these across page, sales, email):
- Short headline: "Pay for the compute you use — predictable per-token pricing, clear performance SLAs."
- Sales one-liner: "Token pricing maps directly to compute and lets you trade off context length, latency, and cost with confidence."
- FAQ snippet: "How do tokens translate to my app? On average 750 characters ≈ 100 tokens. Use our sample-converter tool and a small test to forecast costs for your prompts."

Tier architecture (recommended 3-layer plus enterprise add-ons):
- Trial / Developer (metered, free credits): low friction for exploration, up to X tokens free, limited concurrency, community support.
- Scale (pay-as-you-go): metered token pricing, volume discounts at defined thresholds, throughput-oriented limits and higher SLOs.
- Committed / Reserved (contracted): committed monthly/annual token blocks, deep discounts, dedicated support, burst capacity and predictable latency SLAs.
- Enterprise add-ons (optional list): data residency, private deployment, extended retention, premium on-call and onboarding, custom model pinning.

Naming guidance: use customer-friendly names (Developer, Scale, Committed) rather than technical terms (e.g., Dedicated vs Reserved) in public pages; use internal names in sales decks for precision.

Discounting guardrails (sales and finance playbook):
- Discount levers (approved): term length (12/24/36 months), committed token volume, multi-year prepay, seat bundles for integrations/support.
- Do not use discounts to mask higher base unit pricing. Base list price must be published; discounts applied on clearly visible line items.
- Minimum commitment threshold for custom discounts: $50k ARR equivalent for initial approval (example, adjust by region).
- Max discount tiers: 10% standard, 20% for strategic accounts with technical prerequisites, >20% require VP approval and a commercial plan.
- Bundling rule: discounts may apply to committed token volume only; add-ons (support, private deployment) priced separately or with explicit bundled discount.
- Anti-abuse clause: override or revoke promotional discounts for usage patterns identified as non-production (massive short-term bursts, automated tests), or require conversion to committed terms.

Discount language for customer-facing materials (templates):
- Neutral: "Volume and term commitments unlock additional pricing benefits. Talk to sales for a tailored rate and predictable capacity plans."
- Direct (for pitch): "Commit to a monthly token block and receive up to 20% off list unit price plus guaranteed burst capacity."
- Renewal nudges: "Commit earlier in the renewal cycle to lock a lower unit price for the next term."

Competitive positioning notes (quick map):
- Cloud provider endpoints: often compute-agnostic pricing or VM-hour centric. Key redwood differentiator: per-token unit economics + inference optimizations that lower effective cost without sacrificing latency.
- Single-model API vendors: position against them on observability (per-route cost/latency), and rollout controls (canary, fallback). Emphasize our unified surface across hosted/dedicated/private.
- Self-hosted runtime vendors: we compete on operational burden. Ask procurement about total cost of ownership (ops + hardware) vs committed pricing with Redwood’s SLA.

Sales objection handling (snippet bank):
- "Token pricing is hard to predict" → "We provide a quick estimate tool and sample-conversion templates; plus reserved capacity to make spend predictable."
- "We want per-user pricing" → "We can present a mapped view for your product metrics (cost per DAU, cost per session) derived from token forecasts during POC."
- "We have bursts" → "Committed plans include elastic burst credits; for unpredictable traffic we recommend a hybrid: pay-as-you-go for burst, commit for baseline."

Testing and rollout plan for page copy and tier names (experiments):
- A/B headline test: lead with "Per-token predictability" vs "Predictable inference pricing" and measure click-to-signup conversion among dev signups.
- Sales script variant: measure RFP conversion when presenting a mapped cost-per-feature slide vs raw per-token examples.
- Price sensitivity test: ramp visible list price and offer conditional 10% promo for first 6 months. Track churn and conversion.

Operational notes for finance and product:
- Expose both raw token usage and effective token-adjusted cost after caching/quotas in console billing reports.
- Add a sample-conversion utility in docs that uses current default tokenizer to convert common prompt archetypes into tokens.
- In billing export include columns: model, tokens_in, tokens_out, effective_unit_price, route, region, discount_applied.

Open questions and next steps (action items):
- Build the sample-converter tool and a short how-to doc for sales (owner: Platform DX, due in 3 weeks).
- Legal to draft standard discount appendix and anti-abuse language (owner: Legal, due in 2 weeks).
- Run a 4-week A/B test for headline and one-liner on the public pricing page (owner: Growth, test design due in 1 week).
- Create 3-page sales one-pager with mapped cost examples for internal use (owner: GTM enablement, draft due in 2 weeks).

Notes-to-self and stylistic guidance for copywriters:
- Use outcome language: map tokens to what the customer cares about (per conversation, per search, per message) rather than technical tokens where possible.
- Always include a quick conversion example on any pricing page and a durable link to the converter.
- Avoid aggressive discounts on the public page; frame discounts as "term & volume" incentives, not individual negotiation levers.

Appendix: quick sample conversions (approx):
- Short chat reply (20–50 tokens) ≈ 150–400 characters.
- Medium document embedding query (300 tokens) ≈ 2–2.5k characters.
- Long-context summarization (2k tokens) ≈ 13–16k characters.
(These are examples; link to converter for precise estimates.)

End of draft. Comments welcome — specifically need feedback on discount thresholds and whether we want a publicized per-1k-token list price or a per-1M token list price as the canonical public figure.
